segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants gave us varenyam: worth choosing, said with the tongue curled back. Worth choosing, but what? The answer opens the second line.

Somebody's good news lands in the group chat: early acceptance, dream school, a row of exclamation points. It's possible to be truly glad for a friend and still, for one second, feel a little dimmer. Priya had that second this week. It's a good second to meet the Gayatri's next word. The first line said that, of Savitr, worth choosing, and never said what. Now the second line opens, and here it is: bhargo devasya. The radiance of the god.

Bhargo means radiance, splendor, brilliance. Its full form is bhargas. When a word ending in -as meets a sound like the d of devasya, the -as turns into o. So bhargas devasya becomes bhargo devasya. And with that, everything the first line held open clicks shut: that worth-choosing radiance. Then devasya, of the god. Deva is god; -asya is the ending that says of. Savitur gave the name, devasya gives the title: of Savitr, of the god. Now notice what the verse puts at the center. Not the sun's disk. Not the god's form. The radiance. Something nobody holds and everyone sees by. English versions write glory here, or splendor, or light. Whichever word they choose, the verse turns toward the shining and leaves the thing that shines at the edge of the sentence. Here's why that matters on an ordinary week, in that small second. A radiance isn't a prize split into shares. Two lamps in one room don't dim each other; the room just gets brighter. The verse doesn't promise anyone the news they're waiting for. It points at a light that was never in short supply.

segments.voice: Count, on your fingers, people whose light you've seen by lately: someone who explained something, someone who made a room easier, someone whose good news you're glad about even with the pinch. Give each one a breath. Stop at five, or wherever the time runs out.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gayatri is about the sun's disk in the sky.
what it means: it holds in mind the radiance of the god, the shining itself.
what a scholar hears: bhargas is a neuter s-stem; -as becomes o before a voiced consonant, the same join that turns dhiyas into dhiyo two words later.

notes: Gayatri word by word: bhargo devasya. Grammar stated: bhargas (neuter s-stem), -as becoming o before voiced d; devasya as genitive singular in -asya. Confirm wording for learners.
